thread.title: Apple earnings were saved by the company's new MVP

author: morningstar.com
title: Apple earnings were saved by the company's new MVP
text:
By Therese Poletti, MarketWatch
Opinion: With iPhone unit sales struggling for growth, Apple now depends on all the money iPhone users are spending on apps
Apple Inc. earnings suffered from disappointing iPhone sales, but the world's most valuable company was saved by its once-future, now-current growth engine.
Apple (AAPL) reported fiscal second-quarter earnings that were better than Wall Street had expected (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-stock-rises-after-iphone-sales-fall-short-but-earnings-beat-2018-05-01) Tuesday afternoon. Those results included disappointing revenue and unit shipments for the iPhone, Apple's biggest selling product, as some analysts had predicted (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-earnings-iphone-expectations-are-down-but-anxiety-is-still-high-2018-04-27).
Apple was saved by its software and services segment, the money Apple takes in from app purchases and subscriptions made through the App Store as well as Apple's own services like Apple Music, iCloud and Apple Pay. Apple revenue in that category grew 31% year-over-year to $9.19 billion, far better than the $8.38 billion in revenue that analysts had forecast, according to FactSet.
Apple has been focusing more on this arena in the past year (http://blogs.marketwatch.com/thetell/2017/01/31/apple-earnings-expected-to-rebound-thanks-to-iphone-7-live-blog/) after saying for a while that software and services will be a huge growth area, and executives have projected that Apple will double services revenue from 2016 to 2020. Chief Financial Officer Luca Maestri underscored that goal by pointing out that Apple doubled software and services revenue from the same period four years prior.
Don't miss: Apple is about to get a lot more of your money (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-is-about-to-get-a-lot-more-of-your-money-2016-04-04)
Chief Executive Tim Cook especially paid attention to the number of Apple customers who are subscribing to services through the App Store, which gives Apple steady revenue as it gets a percentage of each monthly bill paid to app developers. Asked for specific drivers of growth in the segment, Cook said it was broad-based both geographically and across services, but pointed out for a second time in the call that paid subscriptions jumped by more than 100 million from a year ago, to 270 million.
Cook also pointed out that Apple Pay is increasing in its use around the world, with active users doubling and transactions tripling. Cook especially called out countries like Japan and China, where it is in use in the widely-trafficked public-transit systems in Tokyo, Beijing and Shanghai.
"This is just a huge opportunity for us and I feel very good about the track we are on," Cook said a bit later in response to another question about services growth.
See also: Reviewers aren't too excited about Apple's HomePod (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apples-stock-rises-even-with-early-homepod-reviews-far-from-raves-2018-02-06)
Cook also highlighted Apple's wearables products in both the company's news release and his comments on the conference call. "Other products" -- which includes the Apple Watch, Beats headphones, AirPods, Apple TV, HomePod and iPod Touch -- also beat expectations, with revenue surging 38% in the quarter to $3.9 billion.
It appears that the HomePod may not be faring so well, however. The only comments Cook made about the smart speaker, which was introduced in February (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-homepod-speaker-to-arrive-feb-9-2018-01-23) (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-homepod-speaker-to-arrive-feb-9-2018-01-23) to rival Amazon.com Inc.'s (AMZN) Echo and Alphabet Inc.'s (GOOGL) Google Home, were that it delivers amazing sound and will change the way people listen to music at home. While Apple does not break out sales in the "Other" category, it does typically give some kind of color about sales, as Cook did for Apple Watch several times in the call; the fact that Cook avoided any such commentary about the HomePod suggests it is not going to be a huge difference-maker for Apple.
The biggest difference-maker for Apple is the iPhone, and many analysts and investors have been speculating that Apple's $1,000 iPhone X has not been selling as well as initially hoped, which has hit the company's stock in recent weeks. In after-hours trading, Apple shares jumped more than 3%, as investors were also pleased with Apple's plans to buy back a massive $100 billion in stock and a dividend increase (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/how-many-billions-is-apple-about-to-promise-its-investors-2018-05-01). Before Tuesday's news, Apple's shares were down about 0.1% so far this year, while the S&P 500 index has declined 1%.
Many of the questions on the company's call were about potential iPhone saturation and efforts to get Cook to talk about future pricing of new iPhones and whether or not the $1,000 price of the iPhone X had been an issue. Cook repeatedly declined to say whether Apple would again aim for a $1,000 price on its top-of the line-iPhone this year, instead focusing on iPhone X being the best-selling iPhone since it was introduced and eventually providing an analogy.
"A team wins the Super Bowl, maybe you wanted them to win by a few more points, but it's a Super Bowl winner," Cook said. "I could not be more proud of it."
Apple can look at Tuesday's earnings the same way -- it won by beating expectations, but the miss on iPhone sales will still be a point of contention with investors and analysts. If Apple is going to repeat the victory in future quarters, its star player may have to be software and services instead of the company's longtime stud, the iPhone.
-Therese Poletti;
 01-18 2008ET
